articles.title: 2 air traffic controllers left work early the night an Air Canada jet collided with a fire truck at LaGuardia, source says
articles.summary: Two LaGuardia Airport air traffic controllers in the control tower left work early the night an Air Canada Express flight collided with an airport fire truck...
articles.body:
Two LaGuardia Airport air traffic controllers in the control tower left work early the night an Air Canada Express flight collided with an airport fire truck on the runway, according to a source familiar with the investigation into the March 22 crash.

The two pilots of Air Canada Express Flight 8646 were killed when the jet collided with an airport fire truck just after landing. The fire truck had been crossing the taxiway to respond to an incident across the airport. The plane had 72 passengers and four crew members on board for the one-hour flight from Montreal to New York's LaGuardia, dozens of whom were injured.

The Federal Aviation Administration is now considering disciplinary action against the controllers, the source said, adding that their departure was not by "just a few minutes." Both FAA controllers are currently on leave, according to the source, and are not currently responsible for controlling air traffic.

The new details were first reported by the Wall Street Journal as the National Transportation Safety Board continues to investigate the crash. The agency's final report —and a finding of probable cause and contributing factors — is not likely to be published for another six months.

"The FAA is committed to holding employees accountable, and we will not compromise the safety or efficiency of the National Airspace System," the agency said in a statement.

The union which represents air traffic controllers, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, would not confirm that controllers were being disciplined, but said the union is "actively discussing these allegations with FAA leadership."

"We believe those discussions are the appropriate forum for addressing the matter," the union said in a statement.

Both NATCA and the FAA are considered parties to the NTSB investigation, which typically muzzles such organizations from commenting publicly on a crash until a final report has been published. CNN has reached out to the NTSB for comment.

"We will not tolerate fraud, and we are taking appropriate action to hold folks accountable and prevent unlawful practices from disrupting the traveling public," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement. "But when a small percentage of individuals take advantage of the American taxpayer, unfairly add additional work to their fellow controllers, and impact the airspace – we have no choice but to act."

articles.title: An Oklahoma woman opened a $1,373 electric bill, including a $598 deposit after late payments; she says it topped her monthly rent and sparked a petition over soaring power costs
articles.summary: US News: When Raelynn McMurchy opened her electricity bill this month, the amount was more than twice her family's monthly rent. The bill totalled $1,373, incl.
articles.body: When Raelynn McMurchy opened her electricity bill this month, the amount was more than twice her family's monthly rent. The bill totalled $1,373, including a $598 security deposit that her power company required after she fell behind on earlier payments. Faced with the choice of keeping the electricity on or paying for other basic needs, the Tulsa resident started an online petition calling for changes to the state's rising energy costs. McMurchy is among a growing number of customers struggling to pay their electricity bills as long periods of extreme summer heat push power use and monthly charges higher across the region. As reported by Scott Horsley for NPR and Ideastream Public Media, electricity prices have risen faster than general inflation, leaving many households facing growing debt and the risk of having their power disconnected.Extreme heat drives up electricity usePublic Service Company of Oklahoma (PSO), the area's main electricity provider, earlier this year asked state regulators to approve a 15 per cent increase in residential electricity rates. Under a proposed agreement reached with the Oklahoma Attorney General's office, the increase was reduced to about 1 per cent. However, even with basic rates mostly unchanged, household bills have climbed because of extreme weather. Tulsa recorded more than twice its usual number of days with temperatures reaching 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37.8 degrees Celsius) this season. The continued heat has forced air conditioners and fans to run for long hours, sharply increasing electricity use.High shutoff rates hurt struggling familiesFor households already finding it difficult to pay their bills, the risk of losing electricity is a serious concern. A US Department of Energy review of utility shutoffs in 2024 found that PSO disconnected customers for non-payment at more than five times the national average rate. In the Tulsa service area, at least 19,000 customers have their electricity shut off each month because of unpaid bills. Some states ban utility companies from disconnecting electricity during periods of extreme summer heat because of the health risks. Oklahoma does not have the same protection. Rules overseen by the Oklahoma Corporation Commission allow power companies to disconnect customers as long as the heat index stays below 101 degrees Fahrenheit (38.3 degrees Celsius). Consumer groups have repeatedly asked state regulators to lower that limit. They argue that dangerously hot indoor conditions can develop well before the outdoor heat index reaches 101 degrees. “I wish every corporation commissioner had to sit in a house that had no electricity when it's 95,” said Joanne Pearson, president of the Helping Hand Ministry in downtown Tulsa.Local charities struggle to meet demandThe growing financial pressure has also placed a heavy burden on community organisations that help residents avoid losing power. At the Helping Hand Ministry office, across from First Presbyterian Church in downtown Tulsa, residents line up every Monday and Tuesday morning with notices warning that their electricity will be disconnected. The charity spends as much as $14,000 a week on emergency assistance. The money comes from local foundations and church donations and is used to help residents delay or prevent power shutoffs. Volunteer John Johnson often contacts PSO's parent company, American Electric Power, to negotiate partial payments for people facing immediate disconnection. In one case, a $350 emergency payment helped retail worker Ashley Fonseca Mejia keep her electricity connected. “It is a relief,” Fonseca Mejia said. “These bills have been skyrocketing.” The problem is not limited to low-income households. Some full-time workers are also struggling to handle sudden increases in their bills. Eric Widger, who works at a nearby Kimberly-Clark manufacturing plant, saw his monthly electricity bill double to around $500. “Payday for me is Friday, and they were going to cut it off Thursday,” Widger said. “I have had it cut off before. It's really heartbreaking because you may have to pay 700 USD or 800 USD just to turn it back on.” Pearson said working families are increasingly being forced to choose between basic needs. “It's like they're jugglers and they've got all these balls in the air,” Pearson said. “Do I pay rent, do I pay the electric bill. Do I feed my family? It's constant, and it's never-ending.” With hotter weather continuing to push up electricity use across the central United States, residents and consumer groups such as McMurchy are calling for changes to security deposit rules and stronger protections against summer shutoffs. They want regulators to act before the next period of extreme heat puts more households at risk of losing power.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Former Gitmo prosecutor likens 9/11 trial delay to 'Frankenstein's zombie court'
articles.summary: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three alleged 9/11 co-conspirators will face trial in June 2028 as the Guantánamo military commission sets new deadlines.
articles.body: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, and three alleged co-conspirators will finally stand trial in 2028, as the case against them has languished amid lengthy delays and a protracted process that one expert has likened to "Frankenstein's zombie court." A military judge on Wednesday set the long-delayed trial for June 5, 2028, while establishing deadlines for the case. Much to the frustration of the loved ones of those who died during the attacks, Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators have been held at a military detention center in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for more than two decades. The problem, according to Michael Lebowitz, a former Guantánamo military commissions prosecutor, isn't the evidence against the terror suspects — it's the system. NEW EVIDENCE IN LOCKERBIE PAN AM FLIGHT 103 BOMBING CASE PUSHES FEDERAL JUDGE TO POSTPONE TRIAL "It's the system and how it evolved and was created. And it's also an issue of Guantánamo Bay itself, where Gitmo is an adequate, albeit expensive, option for things like detaining suspected war criminals and even migrants," Lebowitz told Fox News Digital. "The problem is that we used to call it the traveling circus because, in order to even conduct the smallest court hearing, everybody has to go to Washington, D.C., and get on an airplane," he continued. "I'm talking judges. I'm talking prosecutors, defense counsel, witnesses and court people." TRUMP TURNS TO 'ZOMBIE' COURT AFTER BOASBERG POINTED TO IT IN DEPORTATION FIGHT The case of Mohammed, as well as Walid bin Attash, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Ammar al-Baluchi, has been delayed for decades amid lengthy legal wrangling, including failed efforts to resolve the case through plea agreements. The 2028 date sets a timetable for a case that has remained in pretrial proceedings for years as the military commission has addressed disputes over evidence and other legal issues before a trial on the merits can begin, Fox News Digital previously reported. NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS Mohammed, a Pakistani citizen, is accused of masterminding the attacks in which hijackers crashed commercial airliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon. A fourth hijacked plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to overtake the hijackers. The case has had more than 10 judges, Lebowitz said, meaning lawyers have had to keep relitigating the same "mundane" issues. Lebowitz, an Army veteran, participated in a number of cases in Guantanamo, including the 9/11 case and the bombing of the USS Cole. TRUMP ADMIN INVOKES 30-YEAR DORMANT TERROR COURT AS IT SEEKS TO DEPORT AFGHAN WOMAN TIED TO ELECTION DAY PLOT "What I found was that the way the system has kind of been set up and how it evolved and turned into, it's essentially a candy store for defense lawyers, where the judges don't have teeth to control the courtroom like you would in federal court," he said. "It just goes from there where defense lawyers can really grease up the system and grease up the gears and really grind it to a halt." One issue prosecutors will have to iron out is whether to seek the death penalty, Lebowitz said. Even if Mohammed and the other suspected terrorists are condemned to death, it's highly unlikely to be upheld, he said. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES "You're dealing with cases where, essentially, the defense lawyers would put the CIA on trial for their treatment of detainees after 9/11," he noted. Despite some of the suspected 9/11 suspects finally getting their day in court, families of the victims also want Saudi Arabia to be held responsible. "I think we’d ask the same question about the case against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, whose agents supported al-Qaeda and the terrorist hijackers, too, after they arrived in the U.S., Terry Strada, national chair of 9/11 Families United, told Fox News Digital. In 2024, Mohammed, bin Attash and al-Hawsawi agreed to admit their roles in the terror attacks in exchange for serving life sentences and avoiding the death penalty. While some 9/11 families supported the idea, others blasted the deal. Amid the criticism, the Biden administration withdrew the plea deal, resulting in more litigation. Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller contributed to this report.

articles.title: California pastor charged with yearslong child molestation as investigators seek more victims: DA
articles.summary: David Johnson, an Ojai pastor and massage therapist, faces six felony child molestation charges in Ventura County as investigators seek more victims.
articles.body: A California pastor and massage therapist has pleaded not guilty to charges accusing him of molesting two children under the age of 14 over several years, prosecutors said. David Johnson, 58, of Ojai, faces six felony child molestation charges in Ventura County, according to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office. Investigators are also looking for possible additional victims and have publicly asked anyone with information about Johnson or other possible unreported crimes to come forward. Johnson is accused of molesting two children who were under 14 years old at the time of the alleged abuse. Prosecutors said the alleged abuse occurred over several years at locations in Ojai and Oxnard. SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS Johnson, who worked as both a pastor and massage therapist, had access to the children through a familial relationship, according to prosecutors. Authorities have not publicly identified the children. Johnson faces four felony counts of committing a lewd act upon a child and two felony counts of continuous sexual abuse. Prosecutors have also filed special allegations involving substantial sexual conduct and the victims being under 14 years old, according to the district attorney’s office. EX-TEXAS MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER SENTENCED TO 33 YEARS FOR SEXUALLY ABUSING 13-YEAR-OLD STUDENT Johnson was arrested Monday on charges of child molestation by the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office, according to sheriff’s inmate records. The records show Johnson was arrested shortly before 3 p.m. and booked into the Ventura County Main Jail later that evening. Johnson appeared in Ventura County Superior Court for his arraignment and pleaded not guilty to all six charges. He remains in custody without bail and is scheduled to return to Ventura County Superior Court on Friday for a bail review hearing. HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER WHO ALLEGEDLY HAD SEX WITH STUDENT IN CLOSET NOW FACES CHARGES INVOLVING MORE TEENS Deputy District Attorney Cesar Ponce of the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office Sexual Assault Unit is prosecuting the case. Investigators have not said publicly how many additional victims they believe there could be. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The district attorney’s office is asking anyone with information about the case or other possible unreported crimes involving Johnson to contact Ventura County Sheriff’s Office Detective Michael Loth at 805-384-4745. Fox News Digital reached out to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office for additional information.

articles.title: ICE officer’s gun found in bathroom at San Francisco airport
articles.summary: A flight attendant found an ICE officer’s gun unattended in a public restroom at San Francisco International Airport last month, NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit has confirmed.
articles.body: SAN FRANCISCO — A flight attendant found an ICE officer’s gun unattended in a public restroom at San Francisco International Airport last month, NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit has confirmed. The gun was found in the stall of a men’s bathroom past the security checkpoint in Terminal 2 on the evening of July 21, according to SFO public information officer Doug Yakel. The flight attendant who found it reported the gun to security staff, who closed the restroom to the public and called 911, Yakel said in an email. San Francisco police officers responded within minutes and were on scene when the ICE officer later returned to retrieve the lost firearm, Yakel said. It’s still unclear how long the gun was left sitting in the bathroom before it was found. The airport reported the incident to TSA for potential follow-up action, Yakel added. It’s unclear what the ICE officer was doing at SFO or whether he has faced any discipline. Yakel said the airport wasn’t privy to the nature of ICE’s presence at the airport that evening, and ICE has not responded to questions sent Wednesday morning by NBC Bay Area. Ukrainian immigrant Iryna Gorb was arrested by ICE officers at SFO the following day. Video of her arrest was captured and posted online by Richmond City Council member Doria Robinson. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Gorb lawfully entered the U.S. in 2010 but overstayed her visa by more than 15 years. NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit learned of the ICE officer’s lost gun through a public records request seeking further details on Gorb’s arrest. An internal email contained within a batch of records the airport released this week alluded to an “event where an ICE officer left his gun in the MRR near Checkpoint D in TB2.” The airport provided additional details Wednesday afternoon in response to questions from NBC Bay Area. ICE presence at U.S. airports has made headlines across the country in recent weeks, with immigration attorneys reporting an uptick in airport arrests and warning clients about flying. It’s unclear exactly how many immigrants have been arrested at SFO, but Yakel told NBC Bay Area the airport is aware of three such arrests since March, including the arrest of Gorb. Yakel said the airport is “not involved in decisions about DHS or ICE operations” and doesn’t “assist in immigration enforcement, consistent with Sanctuary City policies.” NBC Bay Area obtained CCTV video of another such arrest on March 22 that also led to widespread public outcry after bystanders filmed the incident and posted it on social media. The third arrest took place on May 1, Yakel said.

articles.title: 'Cowboy builders' targeted in new government clampdown
articles.summary: A database of trusted tradespeople and a system to protect customers' money is being launched by the government next month.
articles.body:
People carrying out home renovations will gain greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards, the government has said.

Traders signing up to the scheme launching next month will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.

The National Federation of Builders said the changes would not stop rogue operators while the Tories suggested there would be added paperwork for firms already operating legitimately.

Citizens Advice has said home renovations are one of its biggest sources of consumer complaints.

The government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months have experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.

It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority suggesting customers lost more £10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.

BBC News has previously reported on "bait-and-switch" locksmith scams , where customers were given an initial cheap quote before hidden charges and unnecessary work were added.

Under the new traders' scheme, customers' money will be held in an account and released in parts after certain milestones in projects are completed.

The National Federation of Builders (NFB) told BBC Breakfast there are already schemes in place to find trustworthy builders.

Adas Rico Wojtulewicz-Richmond, the NFB's director of policy, said: "Is this scheme going to stop bad actors operating and ripping people off? I don't think it will."

He said a better approach would be for every project to have a "passport" which records all the work done.

"It protects consumers because you can find out which companies are doing a poor job, and it brings up the industry standards," he said.

The prime minister said rogue tradespeople gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and would be "putting the cowboys out of business".

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said that, while home improvements can be stressful, "we're taking action to protect consumers, support reputable traders and make sure people can spend their money with greater confidence and security".

Shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith said the announcement looks like "the sort of government initiative that risks the unintended consequence of piling more paperwork onto the majority of businesses who already do the right thing".

He said: "The government would do far better to beef up law enforcement and have tougher sentences for the minority who fraudulently rip off customers. Those who break the rules will keep breaking them regardless of whether there is an app in the way."

Liberal Democrat business spokesperson Sarah Olney said: "Rogue builders cause real harm and ruin real lives every year. The current system is simply not fit for purpose and this half-baked announcement falls frustratingly short from fixing it.

"A voluntary code for tradespeople completely misses the mark. Rogue operators won't voluntarily sign up - they will simply keep exploiting families in the shadows."

Alongside action on rogue tradespeople, the government has announced plans to regulate private bailiffs in England and Wales, to protect people in debt from "intimidating behaviour, unfair treatment or being pushed into excessive repayment arrangements".

Under the changes, people facing enforcement action will have access to an independent complaints process, and private bailiffs will be held to professional standards.

Sarah Sackman, minister for courts and legal services, said bailiffs did an important job, but "with that responsibility must come high standards".

As part of the changes, the government will look at how organisations such as Trading Standards work with regulators and enforcement bodies "so consumers are not passed from pillar to post".

Last year, a Freedom of Information request by Which? revealed that understaffing in trading standards teams was leading to more scams and dangerous products being sold.

articles.title: Edinburgh launches new media event after final TV Festival ends
articles.summary: Edinburgh TV Festival moves to Manchester next year, so what will a new event look like?
articles.body:
Plans for a new Scottish event to replace the Edinburgh TV Festival have been launched.

The industry festival – which ends on Friday – will move to Manchester next year after 50 years in the capital.

But Screen Scotland, the Scottish government and the other Edinburgh Festivals say it is too important to lose.

Speaking at a launch event in Edinburgh, Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan, revealed details of a new initiative which would build on the city's unique position as a global shop window for talent, content and creative ideas.

"We are so proud of Scotland's screen sector," she said. "And this exciting addition to the August festivals line-up will provide a new way to embrace the creativity and cultural innovation which makes our capital unique."

Initial research has already been undertaken with further consultation continuing under former TV festival creative director Rowan Woods.

It is hoped that a pilot version of the new festival will run in August 2027, and that it will be expanded to include those who consume content as well as those who make it.

McAllan said when she was first appointed culture secretary after the election in May, one of the first meetings she had was about the Edinburgh TV Festival.

"There was a collective disappointment about its departure but almost as soon as I was briefed on its departure, I was told 'don't worry minister, we're already on it. We will work together and move on'."

She said she was delighted to announce details of a new TV and screen festival for Edinburgh to sit alongside all the other festivals in August.

Richard Gadd, whose hit Netflix show Baby Reindeer was first discovered at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe told the event his first experience of the Fringe was with his school when they saw a production of Black Watch which was first staged there in 2006.

Four years later, he made his own debut with his solo show 6 And Half A 7 which was staged in a bar. Sometimes the audience was just one person, and he would just buy them a drink.

Later shows were more successful, including Monkey See, Monkey Do in 2016 which won him the Edinburgh Comedy award, and Baby Reindeer in 2019 which led to interest from TV executives from Netflix, BBC, C4 and HBO.

"Everything I have in my life, I owe to this festival, not just the chance to meet agents and producer writers but going full time as a writer," he said.

"A chance to experiment and take risks - to fail spectacularly and come back the next night to start again.

"If the fringe becomes too expensive, too commercial, we could lose the very thing which makes it extraordinary. We could lose the place where someone can arrive with an idea and leave with a career. "

Gadd pointed out that Fleabag, Taskmaster, Six the Musical, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead, Stomp, Flight of the Conchords, Garth Merengue, Alan Partridge, Mr Bean, The League of Gentlemen, Jerry Springer the Opera, Operation Mincemeat, The Mighty Boosh and Black Watch all began there.

"This is so much more than a festival," he said. "It's the cultural backbone of the whole country, the world even, and we must protect it at all costs so everyone who dares to step out their front door and call themselves an artist can be given the same opportunity that I was."

The TV festival began as the Edinburgh Television Drama festival in 1976 – a spin-off from the city's international film festival – founded by its director Linda Myles and Gus MacDonald, a former Granada TV executive.

Myles, the first woman to direct a major film festival was keen to spark ideas and debate about a rapidly changing industry.

Key to its success was its timing in the final week of the world's largest arts festival which allowed delegates to network, while also "shopping" the city for fresh ideas, talent and shows.

As well as Baby Reindeer, Fleabag was first performed as a theatre show before being developed by the BBC, as was Hannah Gadsby's show Nanette in 2017 before being developed by Netflix.

The various comedy awards handed out in the final week, also offer a shortlist for those attending the TV festival.

Since 2001, the TV festival has been run by an independent foundation based in London.

It attracts more than 2,000 delegates and retains some of the original features such as the MacTaggart lecture – named after the ground-breaking drama producer James MacTaggart who had died two years before.

Over the years, it has been delivered by Rupert Murdoch, Ted Turner, Vince Gallagher and David Attenborough.

TV dramatist and writer Dennis Potter used his moment in 1993 to lash out at the BBC's director general John Birt and chairman Marmaduke Hussey, calling them "croak-voiced Daleks" who had a cold and impersonal approach to TV writing.

Presenter Amol Rajan used his Alternative Mactaggart to urge the UK government to "stop dithering" about the BBC's funding structure.

The main lecture was delivered by Pedro Pina, Vice President of YouTube, who gave a reminder about the vast changes in the TV landscape since the festival first began.

But the wider festival ecosystem has also changed.

Concerns over affordability, accessibility and sustainability led to an offer to other UK cities to bid for the chance to host.

Edinburgh repeated its offer but was beaten by Manchester which will host the TV festival from 2027. Details of timings (since it no longer has to coincide with the last weeks of the festivals) and programme have yet to be announced.

There are few details about the Scottish replacement either, except that the consultation will be led by Rowan Woods and will be funded by Screen Scotland and delivered through the Fringe Society.

It is thought the ambition is to create an event which is not industry only, but opens out guest speakers who have included Shonda Rimes, Tina Fey and Gary Oldman, to audiences.

It will also expand its vision beyond traditional film and television output towards global content industries. Scotland has seen expanded interest in recent years with productions such as Outlander (Sony/Starz) and Dept Q (Netflix).

Separately, Screen Scotland plans to establish a new debate in honour of Linda Myles, who co-created that first TV festival.

The Linda Myles Debate will recognise her long-standing belief that Edinburgh is the place for rigorous debate around the screen industries.

"I'm deeply touched and honoured to have the debate named after me," she said.

"It's exciting to see the importance of ideas and discussion being recognised in the plans for the new event, especially as this was the initial intention of the creation of the Edinburgh Television Festival in 1976."

articles.title: Invasive blue crabs cost Italy’s shellfish industry tens of millions of euros; scientists release 130,000 octopuses into Adriatic Sea to keep them in check
articles.summary: Europe News: Italy is turning to an unusual predator in its battle against an invasive species that has wreaked havoc on the country’s fisheries: the common octopu.
articles.body: Italy is turning to an unusual predator in its battle against an invasive species that has wreaked havoc on the country’s fisheries: the common octopus.According to Scientific American, scientists have released around 130,000 young octopuses into the Adriatic Sea as part of an effort to control the growing population of invasive blue crabs, which have damaged shellfish stocks, fishing equipment and coastal fisheries.The initiative, known as Octo-Blu, is being led by researchers at the University of Bologna in collaboration with the Emilia-Romagna regional government.Tiny octopuses released into Adriatic watersThe octopuses currently being released are not fully grown animals but newly hatched “paralarvae”, measuring only a few millimetres. They have been released into coastal waters, where they are expected to mature.The project began in 2024, initially focusing on laboratory work to determine how the young octopuses could be raised successfully in tanks.This summer, researchers released many of the young octopuses into open water near Cesenatico and Riccione, two areas among those particularly affected by the invasive blue crab population.The team has also placed artificial dens on the seabed to provide shelter for the vulnerable young octopuses as they grow.One adult octopus can eat four blue crabs a dayThe strategy relies on the common octopus’ natural appetite for crustaceans. Under suitable conditions, a one-kilogram adult octopus can consume around four medium-sized blue crabs in a single day.Antonio Casalini, an aquaculture research technician at the University of Bologna, said the project is not introducing an unfamiliar predator into the ecosystem.“We are not introducing a new species but working on strengthening the population of a native species already naturally present in the Adriatic,” Casalini said.That distinction is important because the common octopus is already native to Mediterranean waters, unlike the blue crab, which was introduced to the region.Invasive blue crabs have devastated Italian fisheriesBlue crabs are considered a valuable seafood species in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States. In the Mediterranean, however, their growing population has become a major ecological and economic problem.The species arrived in the Mediterranean last century, but its numbers began increasing rapidly about a decade ago.The consequences have been severe for Italian coastal communities, with blue crabs damaging fishing nets and feeding on clam beds and mussel stocks. Hundreds of fisheries along the Italian coast have reportedly been forced to close.The damage to the shellfish industry has cost tens of millions of euros, while the Italian government has invested heavily in attempts to contain and combat the invasive species.Will the ‘octopus army’ work?Despite the ambitious plan, scientists involved in the project acknowledge that releasing thousands of young octopuses does not guarantee that they will survive long enough to become effective predators.According to the reporting, mortality among octopus paralarvae can approach 99.9%, meaning only a very small proportion of those released could eventually reach adulthood.Gianluca Sarà, a marine ecologist at the University of Palermo who is not involved in Octo-Blu, described the concept as “powerful” and “great”, but cautioned that its impact in the real world could ultimately prove “absolutely negligible”.Researchers therefore do not expect the octopuses to eliminate blue crabs from the Adriatic.Casalini said the objective is instead to keep the invasive population under control, with the octopus project forming part of a broader strategy that also includes more aggressive fishing of blue crabs.The experiment represents an unusual attempt to use a native predator to restore some balance to an ecosystem disrupted by an invasive species. Whether Italy’s eight-armed solution can make a measurable difference, however, remains to be seen.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Military veterans told they owe thousands of pounds over clerical error
articles.summary: Hundreds of former UK service personnel have had their pensions cut after being overpaid.
articles.body:
Hundreds of former members of the military have had their pensions slashed after receiving letters telling them to repay thousands of pounds because of a clerical error.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed to the BBC that more than 1000 retired service personnel are being pursued for debts. The majority, 335 veterans, were overpaid a total of £5.1m as a result of incorrect National Insurance calculations.

The Forces Pension Society said it is aware of a small number of veterans whose debts were wiped after raising a formal complaint.

Ray Lawton, 70, was told in July he owed £8,000 following six years of overpayments. Days later, his monthly military pension was cut from £550 to £365.

"I haven't got £8,000 to pay out," said Lawton, who served 16 years in the Royal Artillery.

"I've got a little bit put aside but nowhere near that much."

The Portsmouth-based veteran told the BBC: "I've trusted the army all my life even when I left and I trusted my pension would be right. Then this letter comes and it's just blown it all out."

Lawton's letter was sent from a company called Equiniti, which administers the pension scheme on behalf of the MoD.

It said an error in its system meant he had been overpaid for years.

Lawton is one of many veterans from across the UK who contacted BBC Your Voice after receiving letters out of the blue seeking money they didn't know they owed.

The Forces Pension Society, a not-for-profit which supports military retirees, said it is aware of many overpayment cases running into the tens of thousands of pounds.

A small number of veterans have been told they owe six-figure sums.

The MoD confirmed errors relating to National Insurance adjustments, Pension Sharing Orders (PSO), Early Departure Payments (EDP) and State Pension Age (SPA). It says it is investigating issues on a case-by-case basis.

It added that of the 335 veterans affected by National Insurance errors, a third have paid off their debt in full and 52 have an agreed repayment plan in place. So far, of the £5.1m, £304,000 has been paid back.

Veterans said they want more clarity about the debt and how it has been calculated. Some have called for it to be wiped.

The government said it has a responsibility to recover the funds.

An MoD spokesperson told the BBC that it recognises that errors to pension payments "may cause uncertainty", adding that it is contacting veterans and "providing support for anyone who requires it".

"Where payments have been made in genuine error, we have a responsibility to recover taxpayer funds and will always seek to do so in a sensitive and proportionate way," the spokesperson added.

However, former Conservative defence secretary Penny Mordaunt, said: "While public bodies have a duty to recoup such costs if it makes financial sense to do so, no such assessment has been made in these cases.

"There is a compelling case in many instances for the debt to be wiped".

Lawton does not want the taxpayer to pick up the tab, he is happy to have his pension reduced to the level it should have been but thinks the private company should refund the bill for what he sees as their mistake.

"I think they should take responsibility for it because it's not my fault."

He served 36 years in the Royal Navy and has been told he owes £26,438. As a result, his pension has been cut by around £650 per month.

"I think it's despicable that they are now saying 'yes, we've made this mistake however you're going to pay for it'. How can I forgive the government for that?"

He said: "The financial shock is absolutely devastating and it's still ongoing."

RAF veteran Barrie Goodwin contacted Equiniti six years ago after receiving a higher payment than he was expecting.

He was told the change was because he had reached state pension age. He's since been notified he was overpaid £32,188 and must hand it back.

"I checked, was told it was all correct and now have to repay it," he said. "I'm already cutting back on luxuries. I was helping one of my grandchildren through nursey - that's had to change.

"If the debt isn't waived, I will really struggle."

Equiniti told the BBC it could not discuss individual cases but recognised the concern caused to pensioners.

A spokesperson said it said it was not responsible for the decision to recoup taxpayers' money but "administration of a scheme of this scale involves multiple organisations, systems and processes over many years".

Technology company Sopra Steria has been in charge of the veterans' pension scheme since 2023, and had subcontracted the administration to Equiniti.

A Sopra Steria spokesperson told the BBC that "errors that led to incorrect pension payments originated over a decade before Sopra Steria took over the contract".

The company said it is "working closely with the MoD and Equiniti to ensure robust safeguards are in place for the long term".

The Forces Pension Society is advising anyone who receives an overpayment letter to verify its authenticity, request more information from Equiniti and using the right to complain through the Internal Disputes Procedure.

Additional reporting: Adam Clarkson and Elaine Doran

The Gurkha families fighting for their pensions

articles.title: Selena Gomez pushes back against 'frivolous' fraud claims
articles.summary: Selena Gomez's lawyer says the fraud case is "absurd" - but it is far from unusual for celebrity family business relationships to go wrong.
articles.body:
Selena Gomez's social media accounts brim with adoring fans: two million likes for her most recent post showing her and her husband in a rose-petal strewn hotel, and thousands of comments praising her beauty, her lipstick and the perfume brand she founded.

This week the PR focus for the star – who rose to fame on the Disney channel but has moved into song-writing, films and TV drama – was supposed to be on the upcoming series six of Only Murders in the Building that sees its podcasting sleuths transfered to London for their next adventure.

But the wider chat, outside those friendly spaces, has gone off-script and is largely on a less flattering topic, namely claims from investors who allege she breached her contract by not properly backing the mental health platform Wondermind that she cofounded with her mother five years ago. As a result, the five investors argue, they were defrauded of the nearly $1.2m they invested.

Gomez is pushing back against those allegations - her lawyer has asked that she be dismissed from the case altogether, saying the claims made against her are "threadbare" and arguing she should never have been "dragged into" the case at all.

The investors claim they were told that "Selena Gomez, one of the most famous women on earth, with a billion-dollar brand and a platform unmatched in social media, would be actively building the company as its head of marketing".

Gomez's attorney Matthew Rosengart says their allegations are "vague, generalised and contradictory" and that Gomez never agreed to, and did not, manage the company, or make the kind of commitments they are suggesting.

"The claims against her are meritless if not frivolous," he said.

Mr Rosengart added that the legal team was "exploring other avenues of relief for Ms. Gomez including sanctions against plaintiffs".

The emphatic pushback from Gomez may reflect a concern for her reputation but it also leaves her mother in the hot-seat, facing the fraud allegations alongside the company itself and a third co-founder.

Crisis PR commentator, Lauren Beeching, founder of Honest London says Gomez is far from the first celebrity to try working with a close family member. At times it can come off like in the Jenner-Kardashian household or with the tennis-playing Williams sisters.

But there are plenty of examples - from the Beckhams' to Britney Spears - where family brands and business don't mix well.

Working with close relatives, whether that's a sibling or a parent, or someone else is almost always a higher risk approach, says Beeching.

"It can make the boundaries between the personal relationship with the business and the celebrity's reputation much harder to separate," she says.

The natural level of trust means that you might not apply the same rules as you would in a normal commercial relationhsip, so better guardrails are needed, she says.

"If you're going into business [as a] family, I'd put more structure around it, not less, for sure.

"Define everybody's responsibilities, bring in independent oversight, and decide what happens if something goes wrong before something goes wrong."

"A family relationship shouldn't be a company's governance structure."

At the end of the day Gomez may not need to worry too much over this case, says Beeching

"This will generate headlines because Selena Gomez is enormously famous, but I don't think it's the type of story her core audience is particularly interested in.

"There's an important difference between generating negative headlines and causing lasting reputational damage. "

Still, for celebrities considering trading on their personal brand, she does have words of advice.

"Before lending your name to a company, don't ask what your reputation could do for the business. Ask what that business can eventually do for your reputation as well."

Selena Gomez sued for alleged fraud over mental health company

articles.title: Hypermobility - the little-known 'bendy disease' that causes pain
articles.summary: The disorder may affect hundreds of thousands in the UK, but many face delays in getting a diagnosis.
articles.body:
Vivienne Duval has always been flexible. She can do every yoga pose there is, but it was not until she turned 58 that she realised that this bendiness was not a good thing.

In fact, it was the answer to all of the strange health problems she had been experiencing for years - issues with digestion, fatigue, and pain.

Earlier this year, when Vivienne came across a video on social media explaining the symptoms of Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder, it was like a light bulb switching on.

"I saw myself in everything they were saying," she tells me. "So I armed myself with all the information and went to my doctor."

Vivienne's hunch was confirmed - she had hypermobile joints. "I had all these separate things, but no one had ever put them all together. Now it's blindingly obvious."

The disorder may affect hundreds of thousands of people in the UK, but many - like Vivienne - face significant delays in getting a diagnosis.

Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders (HSD) are connective tissue disorders that cause joint hypermobility - when joints have a greater-than-normal range of motion.

Due to lax collagen between connective tissues, muscles have to work harder to keep joints stable, leading to fatigue and pain, as well as clumsiness.

HSD can also cause gastrointestinal symptoms because the connective tissue within the digestive system is stretchier.

Links between HSD and neurodiversity such as autism and ADHD have also been established.

Some people, like Vivienne, also have hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS), which is diagnosed by looking for hypermobility and faulty connective tissue throughout the body, as well as musculoskeletal issues like dislocations.

Hypermobility disorders may affect hundreds of thousands of people in the UK, though many remain undiagnosed, according to new research from the University of Edinburgh.

It found patients with hEDS and HSD in the UK waited an average of 19 to 21.7 years for diagnosis.

The diagnostic process for HSD is complicated by the fact the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence does not have a dedicated, standalone clinical guideline for diagnosis.

Dr Jessica Eccles, a researcher on brain-body interactions and hypermobility, says diagnosis can be a "postcode lottery in terms of where you are and what opportunities are available to you for assessment".

She adds that HSD and hEDS seem to affect women more. "We know that women's health is not necessarily as well-researched as problems affecting men."

The research found that under a third of those diagnosed said their GP had initiated management for the disorder, and only 13% had access to a "knowledgeable clinician".

This leaves some people feeling as though they have nowhere to go, says Dr Stephanie Barrett, a consultant physician and rheumatologist.

She says "time and time again" she sees people in her clinic who cannot work because of "severe brain fog" linked to hypermobility.

Vivienne is among those feeling unsupported. "I need to be able to help myself and I don't know where to go. I'm finding out about this condition on social media."

Vivienne's mix of frustration and relief over her diagnosis is a reaction I can relate to.

I was diagnosed with HSD earlier this year, and know I am fortunate to have made this discovery at 24 years old, and not years later, like many sufferers.

Vivienne and I both experience joint pain, fatigue, and digestive issues. Growing up, I always thought I was carrying around myriad health problems, but this year, I discovered they were all connected to my bendy joints.

After speaking with my consultant, I found my clumsiness was connected to HSD, that it wasn't normal to wake up every morning already feeling tired, and that, unlike me, most people do not experience pain when standing in a queue or on the train.

Luke Grindlay, 23, was diagnosed with HSD in primary school when teachers noticed he struggled to use pens and cutlery.

He hasn't sought treatment, which he says is probably down to "imposter syndrome", fuelled by a lack of information on HSD.

"If you go online to research this, there's nothing there… I'm going through a lot of pain, but because I can't find anything about it, it's almost like I'm making too much of it."

The unpredictable nature of how HSD can impact me means I relate to this idea of imposter syndrome. Sometimes I can run long distances without too much pain, while other times a shopping trip can tire me out.

Luke works in golf and his role can require a lot of waiting around on courses, which can be painful. However, he says: "It's hard for me to tell people, because not many people know about the condition."

Luke finds the impacts hitting "harder" as he gets older.

Vivienne says her social life and work has been impacted. "I used to work as a massage therapist in work places, but I couldn't stand for long and I would get really tired."

She changed job, and now works as a massage therapist for people living with dementia, which is less physically demanding.

Research suggests HSD symptoms can worsen, or come to light, after a stressor, Dr Eccles says. This might be puberty or menopause, and some papers suggest a link to Covid.

This means someone could go through much of life with flexible joints, but an "external environmental stressor" could come along, worsening everything.

There are ways to treat HSD, Dr Eccles says, but no "single magic bullet". Physiotherapy can be useful, while others may benefit from gentle exercise like swimming.

Dr Barrett explains that physiotherapy can help by "toning up and strengthening the key muscles which hold the skeleton together".

However, she feels the tendency to tell sufferers to "just do a bit of physio" and get on with life is unhelpful. Ultimately, she says more attention needs to be given to HSD and hEDS.

"It takes people working together and sharing ideas, and for the government to recognise this, to tackle this."

articles.title: Why India wants Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman to visit Delhi
articles.summary: India is keen to reset ties with Bangladesh, but old tensions and new regional alliances complicate its efforts.
articles.body:
It is not often that an official email offers a glimpse into relations between two neighbouring countries.

But a message from the Indian president's office earlier this month did just that, quickly catching the attention of diplomats and journalists.

It said a weekend Change of Guard ceremony at the presidential palace had been cancelled because rehearsals were being held for the ceremonial welcome of Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

There was just one problem: no visit had been officially announced.

Within hours, the email was withdrawn . But it added to weeks of speculation over a possible visit by Rahman - and highlighted India's efforts to bring Bangladesh's new leader to Delhi.

Rahman is yet to accept. "No decision has yet been made on the visit," AAM Saleh, the Bangladeshi prime minister's press secretary, told the BBC.

India is keen to host the leader of its eastern neighbour for talks - and the timing matters. This would be Rahman's first visit since taking office after his Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won a landslide victory in parliamentary elections in February.

The vote marked a new political era in Bangladesh after the country's long-time leader Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a mass uprising in August 2024, in which hundreds of people were killed. She fled to India, where she has remained since.

Relations between the two countries deteriorated sharply under the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, which took over after Hasina's removal.

Now, Delhi is hoping Rahman's government offers a chance to reset a crucial relationship - but Hasina's presence on Indian soil is making that harder.

Bangladesh has asked India to extradite Hasina, who was sentenced to death in absentia by a special tribunal for ordering lethal force to be used against protesters during the uprising. She denies the charges.

"We called for the creation of a propitious environment and are awaiting response from the Indian side regarding expediting extradition of Sheikh Hasina," Saleh said.

India says the request is being considered.

Despite the issue, Delhi has made repeated overtures to the new government. A formal invitation was extended to Rahman soon after he took office, and India's High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi has held discussions with Bangladeshi officials, including the prime minister, in recent weeks.

When Rahman visits, Trivedi has said , he will be "accorded the highest honour" and given a "memorable welcome".

Such public enthusiasm is unusual for India, which does not often make such a strong show of wanting to host the leader of a neighbouring country.

"I would imagine that there is a degree of frustration [in Delhi] because except for actually handing over Hasina, they have gone pretty far in terms of reaching out to Dhaka," Shyam Saran, a former Indian foreign secretary, told the BBC.

Saran points to India's efforts to meet some of Bangladesh's immediate needs, including supplying electricity and fuel and issuing medical visas. Several bilateral mechanisms aimed at facilitating trade have also been revived, he said.

Of course, there is a lot at stake for both countries.

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545-mile) border, as well as close cultural and linguistic ties. Bilateral trade was worth more than $12bn last year, overwhelmingly in India's favour.

Bangladesh is also important to India's efforts to improve access to its north-eastern states.

During Hasina's 15 years in power, the two governments expanded road, rail and port links, improving India's access to its north-east. They also worked closely on security, with Hasina's government cracking down on insurgent groups that India said had been operating from Bangladeshi territory.

But India's close relationship with the former prime minister became increasingly controversial in Bangladesh, where critics accused Delhi of overlooking concerns about democracy and human rights.

And her continued presence in India has kept those tensions alive. They resurfaced on 5 August, when Hasina addressed journalists virtually at an event organised by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in Delhi. She vowed to return to Bangladesh in December and accused Rahman's BNP government of suppressing her supporters.

Bangladesh said it was "outraged" that she had been allowed to speak publicly on Indian soil.

India's foreign ministry said it had "no role" in the event and did not "endorse anything said at the forum, especially with regard to the duly constituted government of Bangladesh".

The timing was particularly sensitive. Lailufar Yasmin, a professor at Dhaka University, says there had been reports that Rahman was seriously considering a visit to India before Hasina's appearance.

"It actually created a huge backlash in Bangladesh," she told the BBC. "Questions were raised whether Indian authorities were sincere about a reset in bilateral relationship."

For Rahman, travelling to Delhi while Hasina remains there could therefore carry a political cost at home.

But India's eagerness to repair ties is about more than Hasina. Since her removal, Bangladesh has also begun rebuilding relations with India's arch-rival Pakistan.

Dhaka and Islamabad have exchanged high-level military visits and spoken publicly about expanding defence co-operation - developments being watched closely in Delhi.

In the 2000s, India accused Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence agency of helping train insurgents from India's north-east in Bangladesh and assisting their movement across the border. Authorities in Pakistan and Bangladesh denied the allegations at the time.

The recently announced Mecca pact - a defence agreement signed this month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, three powerful Islamic countries - has also sparked interest from several nations, including Bangladesh.

The specifics of the agreement and the obligations on each party are not clear, but it is modelled on NATO's collective defence principle: that an attack on one member would be seen as an attack on all.

"If there is a security arrangement among Islamic nations in the Middle East, it is not unusual for us to consider participating," Bangladesh's junior foreign minister Humayun Kabir told journalists this week.

Saudi Arabia has also invited Rahman for a bilateral visit. It is not clear whether Bangladesh has been formally asked to join the defence agreement.

Prof Yasmin says Dhaka should proceed carefully. "Bangladesh should be a bit cautious about entering into any defence pact," she says.

"It's not just about antagonising India; Bangladesh needs to wait for a while to see which way it's going and whether it will align with our interests."

For India, these developments are a reminder that its relationship with Bangladesh is changing, and that Delhi can no longer assume the exceptionally close relationship it enjoyed under Hasina.

Rahman's government, meanwhile, has reasons to demonstrate that its foreign policy is not overly dependent on its giant neighbour.

Prof Yasmin says Rahman should visit Delhi before the UN General Assembly meeting in New York in mid-September.

"Neighbours have to live together," she says.

There may soon be another opportunity. India is due to host a BRICS summit in mid-September and Bangladesh has been invited as a special guest.

After weeks of invitations, diplomatic overtures - and one prematurely revealing email - Delhi will be hoping Rahman finally comes.

articles.title: 'We are not wanted anywhere': Rohingya face fierce new wave of hostility in Malaysia
articles.summary: A community that has long felt beleagured is looking over its shoulder again.
articles.body:
Not long ago, Malaysia's then-prime minister urged his country to protect Rohingya Muslims - a stateless minority that has fled violence and discrimination in Myanmar for decades.

"We must defend them, not just because they are of the same faith, but [because] they are humans, their lives have value," Najib Razak said in 2017 .

Nine years on, a fierce new wave of hostility against the Rohingya is sweeping the nation.

So much so that "going to school has become a dangerous thing," says Irhan, a Rohingya refugee, who founded a school in northern Malaysia for children from his community aged six to 15. We have changed his name to protect his identity.

Because Rohingya children are barred from Malaysian public schools, they often attend unlicensed, community-run "learning centres", which are now especially vulnerable.

Irhan's school was raided last month, when eight uniformed police officers stormed inside, took photographs of the students and ordered some of them to go home.

"The students are just here to learn. Now their families are afraid," he says.

A school in Selangor in the west suspended classes for a month and reopened at the end of July with new instructions: students must not wear their uniforms to school and must go straight home after class, without lingering or hanging out in groups.

"We're keeping a low profile to protect our students from getting attacked," says Farooq, a Rohingya teacher.

Crackdowns are haphazard and often spurred by public sentiment. The uncertainty and fear have forced some schools to close in recent months. In some parts of the country, Rohingya have also been evicted from villages they'd been living in for years. Some local residents told Malaysian media that allowing them to remain could lead to "social problems".

After they were evicted from a fishing village near Penang, some120 refugees sought shelter outside the UN's refugee agency in the capital Kuala Lumpur - and were temporarily detained. More than half of them were children.

All of this has left a community that has long felt beleagured looking over its shoulder again.

"In the early years, the Malaysians were our friends. They cared for our children. But it's changed," Irhan says.

"I would leave if I could, but where else can I go? We are not wanted anywhere."

What you need to know about the Rohingya crisis

Landmark Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar heard at top UN court

The UN refugee agency estimates that more than 126,000 Rohingya have resettled in Malaysia, making it the second-largest host country, after Bangladesh, for Rohingya refugees. But some rights groups believe the actual number is far higher.

Rohingya Muslims are denied citizenship in their home country of Myanmar, a predominantly Buddhist state. Although Rohingya trace their roots going back centuries in what is now Rakhine state, successive Myanmar governments have claimed that they are illegal migrants.

Ethnic tensions with the local Buddhist population have flared repeatedly, displacing tens of thousands of Rohingya. They ended up in camps within Myanmar, or fled across the border.

But the biggest exodus began in August 2017, after a brutal military crackdown. The Myanmar army massacred thousands of them, raped Rohingya women and burned their villages.

It was what the UN called "textbook ethnic cleansing" and former US president Joe Biden's administration determined as a genocide. Myanmar is now facing a landmark genocide case at the International Court of Justice, which saw deposed leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi testify.

As Myanmar's leader at the time, she was sharply criticised for how her government responded to the killings, including by playing down what was happening or suggesting that the severity of the violence was exaggerated.

In 2017, more than a million Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. But overcrowded camps, violence and shrinking aid have prompted many to attempt perilous voyages across the Andaman Sea towards Malaysia. These journeys are on cramped, fragile fishing vessels , and thousands die en route.

As more and more Rohingya arrived on its shores, Malaysia's welcome has worn thin.

Although it has never formally recognised asylum seekers – which means refugees have no right to housing, employment, and education – many Rohingya still see Muslim-majority Malaysia as a place of safety and economic opportunity.

Or at least that has been the case for a long time, when Malaysian leaders urged their people and Muslim nations to protect the community.

During the pandemic, the Rohingya were accused of spreading the virus and competing with locals for jobs. Petitions calling for their deportations flooded social media, and authorities turned away hundreds of Rohingya asylum seekers who had been drifting at sea for weeks .

The vitriol has returned with greater intensity this year, inflamed again by social media.

In May, posts emerged online accusing refugees of not properly disposing of animals sacrificed during the Muslim festival of Eid al-Adha and quickly went viral.

These snowballed into unfounded and hyperbolic claims that the community is demanding automatic citizenship, seeking political power, and trying to "take over" Malaysia.

An online petition urging authorities to "Remove Rohingya from Malaysia" garnered more than 420,000 signatures before it was taken down following criticism from rights groups.

Karim, a Rohingya activist, says locals' hospitality had "made [him] feel safe" when he first arrived in 2003.

"Life as a refugee is tough. It's disappointing to be stuck working in construction all these years. However, I found Malaysians to be very friendly and kind, which made me feel safe," says the 45-year-old, who now lives in Penang.

"Now, however, life has become increasingly difficult. I am often afraid to go outside. I've been asked several times while on my commute, 'Why are you making a mess of our city? Why don't you go back?'"

Irhan, who came to Malaysia in 2001 as a teenager among an earlier wave of asylum seekers, feels the same.

Both say most Rohingya want to go back to Myanmar eventually, but at this point they would be returning to a country locked in a bloody civil war .

Their home state of Rakhine has suffered catastrophic destruction amid intense fighting between the military regime and the Arakan Army. For the displaced Rohingya, going home could also mean being forcibly conscripted to fight for the embattled junta , or becoming targets of the Arakan Army.

The UN released a report by an independent fact-finding mission this week detailing how the the plight of minories has "plummeted to a new low" in Myanmar.

The Rohingya are "suffering misery and cruelty on multiple levels and across the country that is heartbreaking", the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on Tuesday.

And Malaysia too has become less of a haven than they had hoped.

Some say they are being used as easy scapegoats for the rising cost of living , with the hostility concentrated on them because they form the largest group of asylum seekers.

"I'm not saying that all Rohingya are good. There are good and bad people in every community. So why should a few individuals' actions be used to typecast a whole community?" Farooq says.

"I escaped the genocide in Myanmar hoping to find safety. Instead, many Rohingya today continue to live with fear of simply being who we are," he adds.

During a campaign speech in July, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, owing to "good relations" between the two countries.

Anwar added that he had warned the Rohingya not to disrupt the lives of Malaysians. "This is our country. Malaysia is our country. Let no one else interfere," he said.

It is perhaps a sign of how mainstream anti-Rohingya rhetoric has become.

Nurulhidayah Zahid, daughter of Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, for example, compared the community to "monkeys in the forest".

"Enough of using religious and humanitarian sentiments. Do good in moderation. Don't let the monkeys in the forest be fed, [while] the children at home die of hunger," she wrote in a post on Threads that includes a picture of Rohingya.

A former deputy police chief, Ayob Khan Mydin Pitchay, likened the influx of Rohingya as a "cancer" requiring urgent action.

The BBC has reached out to the Malaysian prime minister's office and foreign ministry for comment.

Some believe the hostility against the Rohingya will only intensify as Malaysia heads towards the general election, which must be held before February 2028.

"[Refugees and migrants] are once again being turned into convenient political scapegoats to divert attention from deeper domestic challenges," says Yap Lay Sheng, a researcher from the human rights group Fortify Rights.

"For years, the Malaysian government has sought to present the country internationally as a humane and compassionate Muslim nation. Its treatment of the Rohingya exposes the hollowness of that claim," says Yap, who is based in Malaysia.

Back in the industrial building that for several months served as his classroom, Irhan is concerned less about the shifting politics than about what comes next for his students.

"I don't know where to get help, or who can get us registered as a school," he says. "I hope the Malaysians can understand that the children just want an opportunity to learn."

More than 500 Rohingya vanished at sea - what happened?

The college scam that promised students fleeing war a new life in Finland

'We will vote but not with our hearts': Inside the election staged by Myanmar's military rulers

Myanmar's army massacred Rohingyas. Now it wants their help

articles.title: Temporais atingem o Sul nesta sexta; calor aumenta no Sudeste | G1
articles.standfirst: Em São Paulo, a Defesa Civil estadual prevê calor intenso até segunda-feira (31), mas o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) não classifica o período como onda de calor. No Sul, temporais avançam sobre SC e PR.
articles.summary: Rio Grande do Sul tem risco de chuva forte, granizo e volumes elevados. Santa Catarina e Paraná entram na rota dos temporais no fim de semana.
articles.body:
Nuvens carregadas vistas em Porto Alegre (RS). — Foto: Duda Fortes/Agência RBS

A chuva forte continua no Rio Grande do Sul nesta sexta-feira (28). Há risco de temporais , granizo , rajadas intensas e volumes elevados em algumas áreas.

Ao longo do fim de semana, essa faixa de chuva se desloca para Santa Catarina e o Paraná, acompanhando o deslocamento de uma frente fria .

Já no Sudeste e no Centro-Oeste, o sol aparece com mais força , as temperaturas sobem e a umidade do ar cai para níveis bastante baixos em algumas áreas.

Em São Paulo, esse aquecimento será mais forte nos próximos dias. A Defesa Civil estadual prevê calor intenso entre esta sexta e segunda-feira (31), com máximas que podem chegar aos 40°C no interior e aos 36°C na capital paulista.

⚠️ Até a última atualização deste texto, porém, o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia ( Inmet ) não classificava o período como uma onda de calor.

Pelo critério do órgão, as temperaturas precisam ficar pelo menos 5°C acima da média por cinco dias consecutivos, o que não deve ocorrer desta vez, já que uma nova frente fria deve derrubar as temperaturas a partir de terça-feira (1º).

Segundo a Climatempo, por causa dessa frente fria que atua no Sul, há previsão de chuva forte em pouco tempo, tempestades e volumes elevados, especialmente na Campanha, no Sul, na Costa Doce, na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre e em trechos do litoral gaúcho.

Em alguns pontos, os acumulados podem passar de 140 milímetros em 24 horas .

Além da chuva forte, há risco de granizo e rajadas de até 90 km/h em áreas de RS, SC e PR, com mar agitado no litoral gaúcho e catarinense.

No fim de semana, os temporais perdem força no Rio Grande do Sul e se concentram mais em Santa Catarina e no Paraná, onde a frente fria avança entre sábado (29) e domingo (30).

Já no Sudeste, as temperaturas voltam a subir nesta sexta-feira após o frio do início da semana. S

ão Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e Minas Gerais terão mais sol e pouca chuva. Na capital paulista, a máxima pode chegar aos 31°C , e o calor aumenta no fim de semana, com até 36°C em áreas do estado.

No Rio de Janeiro (RJ), a sexta começa com possibilidade de nevoeiro, mas o sol ganha espaço ao longo do dia e a máxima pode chegar a 31°C. Em Belo Horizonte (MG), o começo do dia ainda terá mais nuvens, seguido por períodos de tempo firme, com temperatura perto dos 28°C.

No Centro-Oeste, a sexta e o sábado serão de predomínio de sol, calor e pouca chuva. A maior parte de Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Goiás e do Distrito Federal terá tempo seco, com apenas pequenas áreas sujeitas a pancadas isoladas.

Pedestre se protege do sol na Zona Norte da capital paulista. — Foto: ROBERTO CASIMIRO/FOTOARENA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Cuiabá (MT) aparece novamente entre as capitais mais quentes do país, com máxima ao redor de 40°C nesta sexta e possibilidade de atingir 41°C nos próximos dias.

Campo Grande (MS) pode chegar aos 33°C, também sem previsão de chuva significativa durante boa parte do dia.

A baixa umidade será um dos principais problemas na região. Em Mato Grosso do Sul, Goiás, Distrito Federal e partes de Mato Grosso, os índices podem ficar entre 12% e 20% durante as horas mais quentes.

Esse ar muito seco favorece a propagação de queimadas e pode provocar desconforto, principalmente no período da tarde.

O vento também ganha força em Mato Grosso do Sul. Há previsão de rajadas entre 50 e 70 km/h em áreas do estado, com possibilidade de picos próximos de 90 km/h em alguns pontos.

Temperaturas mínimas previstas para esta quinta em todo o Brasil. — Foto: CPTEC/Inpe

No Nordeste, o tempo permanece mais firme em grande parte da região. As principais áreas de chuva ficam próximas ao litoral, com pancadas previstas entre o Ceará e a Bahia.

Trechos dos litorais do Rio Grande do Norte e da Paraíba podem receber chuva mais forte.

Também há chance de pancadas no interior do Ceará e no oeste do Maranhão, mas a maior parte do interior nordestino terá outro dia de sol e calor.

O ar seco continua chamando atenção principalmente no oeste da Bahia e no sul do Maranhão e do Piauí, onde a umidade pode ficar entre 20% e 30%. Teresina (PI) aparece entre as capitais mais quentes, com máxima que pode alcançar 38°C.

Na Região Norte, as pancadas mais fortes ficam concentradas principalmente no Amazonas e em Roraima. O norte, centro e oeste amazonense podem ter chuva moderada a forte, com risco de temporal isolado em alguns pontos.

Também pode chover de forma mais irregular no Acre, em Rondônia, no Pará e no Amapá. Já no Tocantins, o tempo permanece mais seco e quente, com umidade baixa durante a tarde.

O calor continua forte também em boa parte da região. Palmas (TO) e Porto Velho (RO) podem chegar a 38°C.

articles.title: Veja fotos das enchentes no Nepal | G1
articles.standfirst: Desastre atingiu vilarejos, estradas e prédios após uma avalanche de gelo e rochas provocar uma enxurrada. Imagens mostram a extensão da lama após as enchentes.
articles.summary: Desastre atingiu vilarejos, estradas e prédios após uma avalanche de gelo e rochas provocar uma enxurrada. Imagens mostram a extensão da lama após as enchentes.
articles.body:
Um menino observa a devastação causada por uma enchente repentina às margens do rio Trishuli, no distrito de Nuwakot, no Nepal, na quarta-feira, 26 de agosto de 2026. — Foto: AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha

Continua nesta sexta-feira (28) o resgate das vítimas da avalanche de rochas, lama e gelo atingiu nesta semana região da fronteira entre o Nepal e o Tibete , na cordilheira do Himalaia. A inundação repentina destruiu casas, pontes e estradas próximas a rios.

O número de mortos do desastre passa de 360. Além disso, quase 1500 pessoas seguem desaparecidas.

O Serviço Geológico dos Estados Unidos chegou a apontar que havia ocorrido um terremoto na região. Mais tarde, no entanto, o órgão esclareceu que o tremor havia sido provocado pelo colapso de uma geleira.

Após o deslizamento, a avalanche desceu pela parte mais alta da montanha, arrastando rochas, gelo e água armazenada em reservatórios naturais.

Depois, todo esse volume chegou ao canal do rio Lhende Khola.

A enchente provocada pela avalanche avançou sobre áreas povoadas.

Especialistas alertam ainda Número de mortos em enchentes e deslizamentos na fronteira entre Nepal e Tibete já passa de 360 Um bloqueio de detritos permanece em uma área mais alta do rio na fronteira entre Nepal e China.

Equipes de resgate usam uma máquina de terraplenagem para levar uma vítima de uma enchente no Nepal, na quarta-feira, 26 de agosto de 2026. — Foto: AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha

articles.title: Como escolher materiais para áreas de maior circulação | G1
articles.standfirst: Pisos e revestimentos adequados ajudam a preservar os ambientes por mais tempo.
articles.summary: Pisos e revestimentos adequados ajudam a preservar os ambientes por mais tempo.
articles.body:
Corredores, salas, cozinhas e áreas integradas estão entre os espaços mais utilizados da casa e, por isso, exigem atenção especial na escolha dos materiais. Além da estética, características como resistência, facilidade de limpeza e desempenho no uso diário fazem diferença para manter esses locais bem conservados ao longo do tempo.

Em áreas de maior circulação, a especificação correta dos revestimentos contribui para reduzir o desgaste provocado pelo uso contínuo. Avaliar aspectos como resistência, acabamento e indicação de aplicação ajuda a evitar substituições precoces e garante melhor desempenho durante toda a vida útil do material.

Áreas de maior circulação exigem materiais preparados para o uso contínuo da casa — Foto: Acervo Internet

Outro ponto importante é a facilidade de manutenção. Pisos e revestimentos adequados tornam a limpeza mais simples, preservam a aparência por mais tempo e oferecem mais praticidade para a rotina. A combinação entre desempenho e funcionalidade também contribui para reduzir a necessidade de intervenções ao longo dos anos.

Materiais resistentes e de fácil manutenção ajudam a preservar os ambientes e facilitam o dia a dia — Foto: Acervo Internet

Escolher os materiais certos para áreas de maior circulação significa pensar no uso diário da casa desde o início do projeto. Decisões bem orientadas ajudam a preservar a qualidade dos espaços, reduzir manutenções e garantir resultados que permanecem por muito mais tempo.

articles.standfirst: Sertanejo fez xingamento no momento em que Marrone pediu ajuda a Cuiabano Lima com placa de título de cidadão barretense recebido no dia anterior. No fim da apresentação, disse que era brincadeira.
articles.summary: Sertanejo fez xingamento no momento em que Marrone pediu ajuda a Cuiabano Lima com informações sobre homenagem na Câmara Municipal.
articles.body:
Uma zoeira com clima de treta no fim do show de Bruno e Marrone na Festa do Peão de Barretos 2026 confundiu o público que acompanhava a apresentação da dupla na madrugada desta sexta-feira (28) (assista acima) .

A confusão começou quando Marrone, que recebeu o título de cidadão barretense na última quarta-feira (26) em Barretos (SP), começou a agradecer a homenagem diante dos fãs na arena. Bruno alertou o parceiro de que a dupla precisava entregar o palco por causa das outras atrações - Gustavo Mioto e Rionegro & Solimões estavam escalados.

Mas Marrone seguiu com o discurso e ainda pediu ajuda ao apresentador Cuiabano Lima para lembrar o nome do vereador responsável pela homenagem.

"Ah, não, o Cuiabano também. Agora acabou o resto do show. Pode falar pouquinho, fala pouco porque tem outros shows", disse Bruno.

O apresentador começou a fazer um discurso, enaltecendo Marrone pela trajetória musical e pelo talento dele. Cuiabano pediu uma salva de palmas ao artista. Enquanto ainda falava, foi interrompido por Bruno, que fez um xingamento.

A declaração acabou confundindo o público. Apesar de Cuiabano ter deixado o palco rindo, parte da plateia entendeu o xingamento como coisa séria.

O show seguiu por um tempo antes da despedida. Nos momentos finais, Bruno falou ao microfone, enfatizando que o tom foi de brincadeira, tranquilizando os fãs.
